rows.subtype: Sustained and fleeting smiles in play [Expressing]
rows.description: A toddler flashes a fleeting smile at a peekaboo surprise and a sustained one during a favourite game, showing joy that rises and fades quickly. Short smiles are normal and not a sign of disinterest.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: joy, interest, surprise

rows.description: A toddler stares with the jaw dropped in wonder or while concentrating, and drools while teething. It shows attention or discomfort, not disrespect.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: admiration, curiosity, awe

rows.subtype: Eyes shut against a scary scene [Regulating]
rows.description: A child squeezes the eyes shut or hides them during a frightening part of a film to control fear. It is a healthy way to cope, and adults can offer a hand or a break.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A preschooler nods to agree or answer, although a nod may just mean I heard you rather than I agree. Adults confirm understanding with a question.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A school-age child sees a classmate narrow the eyes and reads suspicion or anger, though the person may be squinting at a bright board. Checking the context, such as light and vision, avoids unfair conclusions.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A school-age child sees a friend lift one shoulder and reads uncertainty, shyness or a half-hearted maybe. It is a weak signal, so asking clarifies.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Averting gaze as avoidance or respect [Interpreting]
rows.description: A teenager reads a peer's averted gaze cautiously: it may mean shyness, guilt, social anxiety, autism-related comfort, or cultural politeness. Asking gently beats assuming dishonesty or disinterest.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: admiration, anxiety, guilt, shyness

rows.description: A teenager opens the arms for a friend who is upset, offering comfort, and learns to ask first if a hug is welcome. Consent applies to every hug, and a refusal is respected.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Prolonged eye closure in exhaustion or calm [Mismatch]
rows.description: A young adult closing the eyes for long moments in a meeting may be tired, meditating, listening intently or overwhelmed. The same sign has several meanings, so a gentle check-in is better than guessing.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26
related mind states: tiredness, calm, overwhelm

rows.subtype: Wet or squeezed eyes under pressure [Regulating]
rows.description: An adult blinks quickly, squeezes the eyes or looks up to hold back tears at work, a common way to regulate strong feeling. A short break to breathe often helps more.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22
related mind states: relief from stress
